transcript: Well, and I would even expand it beyond that. I think it's bigger than just the Freedom Caucus. You have so many factions, essentially we're operating within coalition government. There's so many different, they call us the five families. I would venture to say there's more factions than just five, including a group of free agents, of which I consider myself to be one. It's important that leadership, particularly with these numbers, and not just even in this particular Congress where we have such a slim majority, but in all, all Congresses, they respect every member in their opinion, because at any moment, particularly these times where social media is so dominant, You can have a member who will say and do something completely extravagant and wild and do it for clicks and views and shares and small dollar donation fundraising. I call it the anger-tainment model that many of my colleagues have adopted. But I would say, having experience with the Freedom Caucus, part of the challenge is that being a member of the Freedom Caucus means that you have to turn your vote card over to the group. You have a requirement as a member of Freedom Caucus to not only pay thousands of dollars to join the organization, but then you have to vote with them 80% of the time. My constituents back home in Florida's third, they own my voting card. No group, no other member, no specialty interest group has my voting card. Only my constituents control my voting card. In large part, one of the reasons why I am not a member, but I am considered Freedom Caucus adjacent. To that end, many of my friends are members. And as I talk to them on AG issues, I continually come back to, historically, the Freedom Caucus has voted in a large block against the Farm Bill. And of course, we can all talk about the nutritional side of where the lion's share of spending goes towards. In this case, the Farm Bill that we're working through is 82% nutritional. And you just take a step back from that, the amount of money that's going into the actual food production and the people who are putting the food on the shelf versus the people who are taking the food off the shelf, it is just fundamentally unbalanced. And for so many producers around the country, it's becoming an untenable situation. So I ask my Freedom Caucus friends to think of the Farm Bill as a national defense strategy, because a nation that cannot feed itself is not secure. And so rather than trying to attack food production and farm programs that are the very basic safety nets, the very basic elements that allow people who have so much skin in the game and so much risk out in the fields. I asked them to think of it in those terms rather than how it has been framed over the years and I would say even decades at this point of corporate subsidies. So I think that that's an element of the discussion that we need to be talking about when we're talking about my conservative friends, because I have a lot of conservative friends that are supporting the Farm Bill, but particularly when it comes to House Freedom Caucus, they have stood in opposition to it.

transcript: I don't think anyone has the connectivity they need if you're in rural America today. I mean, my goodness. But it's wild to me that in 2023, we do not have every single American connected to high speed, reliable, and affordable internet. And they have figured out a way to do it without federal assistance. That, I think, is the path forward, which really is a shame because taxpayers have now been put on the hook for so many billions of dollars, but it tends to get lost in all the red tape.
